newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan considers freeing cement investment in China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan considers freeing cement investment in China.

text.p: Taiwan's economics ministry said on Friday it was considering allowing local firms to invest in rival China's cement industry, a move that would benefit Taiwan cement makers whose local mining rights are expiring.

Local media said on Friday the ministry's Industrial Development Bureau had agreed in principle to allow all cement investments in China. Up to now, such projects have been subject to case-by-case reviews.
A ministry spokesman quoted economics vice minister Yin Chi-ming as saying, "Cement investments in the (Chinese) mainland will not be banned."
Yin on Wednesday ordered the bureau to review its policy on cement investments in mainland China, the spokesman said.
Bureau officials said the agency was reviewing a proposal to ease the policy.
"We are still discussing the proposal but have yet to reach a conclusion," a bureau official quoted deputy bureau head Ho Ming-liang as saying.
Taiwan, which has banned direct links with China since a civil war split them in 1949, has allowed a range of "indirect" investments under a political thaw dating to the late 1980s.

Local newspapers said the opening would give local cement makers "a way to survive" after the economics ministry in late May reaffirmed its commitment to end all mine exploration rights in western Taiwan at end-1997. That move aimed to promote cement-making Taiwan's relatively underdeveloped east.
Officials declined to comment on the proposal's intent.

The possible policy change came to light after Taipei said on Wednesday it would allow Taiwan firms to engage in a wider range of investments in arch rival China, while also slapping an outright ban on real estate and large power plant projects.

The liberalisation gave a green light to 411 categories, including travel agencies, recreation facilities, warehouses, hotels, merchandise agents, rental businesses, saunas, printing machines, sewing machines and car and motorcycle parts.
There remain 2,477 items in a more restrictive discretionary category for which case-by-case approval must be sought.
Property and power plant projects were moved from discretionary to a "ban list" -- 299 items where China investments by Taiwan interests remain forbidden.
Altogether, 4,350 investment types are permitted, though capital must be routed through Hong Kong or a third country.

In its drive to avoid becoming economically vulnerable in its rival's economy, Taipei in May banned investment in mainland infrastructure -- chiefly water works, railways, harbours, airports, roads and power plants.
